items.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: The first guy, pretty much, that I worked with was Henry “Red” Allen

ctx.x: Your bandmates today have said the same thing, almost verbatim. And they feel that most of the instructors that are teaching now grew up on Parker and Coltrane, so that’s where they feel — © Fillius Jazz Archive -6-

Well it also has a political thing and it has a racial bias too, to be honest, let’s face it. They think jazz is black primarily, well I’m not going to argue that I think that the greatest practitioners have been black musicians — no doubt or question about it — but before that, there were also people playing together. And you know, whites and that. Sadly whites had a monopoly on the radio and the recordings and that kind of stuff. There certainly was a racial barrier there. But blacks were recording very much…

items.title: Keith Ingham interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997
items.q: he says, “you know these tunes and you play good, you’ll be fine.” So he actually tried, and the musicians union here wouldn’t let it happen... I knew a lot of tunes with Red

ctx.x: Well eventually, like Shearing and Marian McPartland, you decided that you wanted to come here?

Yeah, well I was playing with these Americans — and I keep digressing — I was playing with these Americans and they said “come over to the States.” Actually it was Red Allen, when he came over there, he wanted to bring me back to America. Now this was what ‘64 I think. And Red died in ‘67. And to be honest, I mean I knew a lot of tunes with Red and I thought my God I can’t go there. I mean it’s like throwing into the deep end you know. And he says, “no, come on, I want you to come and be part of my quartet at the…
